title: The Rook Belongs Behind the Passed Pawn
subtitle: Tarrasch's rule, and what happens when you ignore it
summary: Siegbert Tarrasch's guideline is one of the most repeated rules in endgame theory: a rook belongs behind a passed pawn — your own to push it, the opponent's to blockade it. This position shows why: a rook that blocks a passed pawn from the front runs out of squares as the pawn and the enemy king advance together.

rootAnnotations.title: Tarrasch's rule
rootAnnotations.body: 'Rooks belong behind passed pawns — one's own, in order to support their advance, and the opponent's, in order to impede it.' White's rook on c1 already follows the rule: as the pawn advances, the rook's scope down the open file only grows, and it's never in the pawn's way. As a general guideline (not an absolute law — there are well-known exceptions) it holds remarkably often, and this position shows exactly why.

annotations.title: Bringing the king up
annotations.body: With the rook already well placed behind the pawn, White's only remaining job is to walk the king up in support.

annotations.title: The natural-looking blockade
annotations.body: This is most players' instinct: put the rook directly in the pawn's path. It stops the pawn cold for the moment — but notice it also ties the rook to one square on one file, with the enemy king free to come and attack it directly. A rook behind the pawn never has to worry about that.

annotations.title: Staying active instead of blockading
annotations.body: Rather than tying itself to the c-file, the rook stays mobile and starts giving checks — the reverse of the front blockade. This won't save the game by itself (a lone rook still can't hold forever against a supported passed pawn), but it puts up real resistance: it costs White a tempo right away, something the front-blockading rook was never able to do even once.

annotations.title: The contrast
annotations.body: Compare the two rooks here with the main line at the same moment: there, White's king was already attacking a helpless, cornered rook. Here it has had to spend a move reacting to a check instead. A rook kept behind — active, out of the king's reach — is simply a harder problem than one boxed in ahead of the pawn, even when neither one can fully stop the pawn alone.

annotations.title: Attacking the blockader
annotations.body: This is the difference in action: White's king simply walks up and attacks the rook, something it could never do to a rook sitting safely behind the pawn on c1. The rook has exactly one square left that keeps blockading — everywhere else abandons the c-file, and the pawn runs.

annotations.title: Out of squares
annotations.body: Forced — c8 is the only square left on the file, and it's also the pawn's own queening square. A rook that started behind the pawn would never be herded into a corner like this; it always had the whole rest of the board behind it to retreat into. This one has nowhere further to go.

annotations.title: The front rook has run out of squares
annotations.body: The king attacks the rook again, and this time there is no retreat left on the file at all — c8 was the last one. Any rook move now abandons the blockade outright, and the pawn queens or wins material by force soon after. This is the practical cost of a rook in front of a passed pawn: it isn't just passive, it can be hunted down and out of squares entirely, something that essentially never happens to a rook that stayed behind.
